summary: radiation dose is what the Radiation dose calculator works out, and it gets there from your body's internal radiation, the cosmic radiation, the terrestrial radiation and the I smoked. It suits an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Radiation dose calculator work?
sections.html:
The Radiation dose calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports radiation dose in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the terrain elevation, lived next to a nuclear plant? and lived next to a coal-powered plant?); then you type in your body's internal radiation, the cosmic radiation (sea level), the terrestrial radiation and the I smoked.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Radiation dose calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Radiation dose=(3577 ÷ 400) × I smoked + your body's internal radiation + cosmic radiation (sea level) + terrain elevation + (9 ÷ 10000) × lived next to a nuclear plant? + (3 ÷ 100) × lived next to a coal-powered plant? + 7 × lived in a stone ÷ concrete ÷ brick house? + (1 ÷ 125) × had a smoke detector? + (3 ÷ 1000) × used gas lantern mantles? + (1 ÷ 500) × had your luggage X-ray scanned? + terrestrial radiation + worked as a radiation worker + 13 × mammograms + 6500 × thyroid ablation with radioactive iodine + (1 ÷ 1000) × travelled + 40 × number of X-rays + 1000 × CT scans: pelvis ÷ abdomen + 800 × CT scans: chest + 200 × CT scans: head + (7 ÷ 100) × wore porcelain crowns ÷ veneers ÷ false teeth + (3 ÷ 1000) × passed though

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in years, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Time, opening in years
  • %, opening in percent
  • %, opening in percent
  • %, opening in percent
  • %, opening in percent

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Radiation dose calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — your body's internal radiation, the cosmic radiation and the terrestrial radiation — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Radiation dose calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns radiation dose, derived from your body's internal radiation, the cosmic radiation and the terrestrial radiation. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Radiation dose calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for your body's internal radiation, the cosmic radiation, the terrestrial radiation and the I smoked, which is 21 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter travelled in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Travelled opens in kilometers and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (14 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Radiation dose = 2515842 yrs. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Radiation dose calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
